prompt.context: Our client, Little Bud Co, is a beer company in a small country in Latin America. Little Bud and its main competitor, Geineken, are the only players in the market. Geineken's operations are significantly bigger than Little Bud.
prompt.question: Little Bud's CEO has asked us to provide him with strategic options for the company and a recommendation on what he should do. What strategic options would you recommend to the CEO?

clarifying_info.a: Think about what the goals of any company are — ultimately, maximizing shareholder value.
The market is mature; growth is low.
10% of sales are made through large retailers and 90% through bars, restaurants, and small retailers.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other competitors or market segments?
clarifying_info.a: Focus on the regular beer market. The market for small brewers/specialty beers is very small and can be disregarded.

exhibits.title: Revenues by Channel
exhibits.shows: Bar or table showing revenues broken down by distribution channel (large retailers vs. bars/restaurants/small retailers) for the market or for each player
exhibits.data: Revenue figures in USD millions by channel

exhibits.title: P&L for Little Bud and Geineken
exhibits.shows: Partial P&L table comparing Little Bud and Geineken with some line items filled in and others blank
exhibits.data: Little Bud ($M): Revenues 100, COGS 30, Gross Profit 70, G&A 10, Sales & Distribution 30, Marketing 25, EBITDA 5; Geineken ($M): Revenues 700, EBITDA 150 (other line items to be calculated)

exhibits.title: Gross Profit Detail
exhibits.shows: Table comparing unit price and COGS per unit for Little Bud and Geineken
exhibits.data: Little Bud: Unit Price 100, COGS 30, Gross Profit (to be calculated); Geineken: Unit Price 110, COGS 28, Gross Profit (to be calculated)

framework: Revenue: analyze market size by distribution channel (large retailers vs. bars/restaurants/small retailers), pricing, and product mix
Competition: compare financials (P&L), operations, and pricing between Little Bud and Geineken; evaluate buy/sell options
Costs — Fixed: plant & equipment, distribution, marketing
Company: supply chain efficiency, economies of scale, adjacent geographies or related markets

questions.prompt: Given the P&L data in Exhibit 2, calculate the missing Geineken line items and compare margins between Little Bud and Geineken. What explains the margin differences?
questions.guidance: Candidate should fill in Geineken's P&L using percentages consistent with Exhibit 3/context, then compare % of revenue. Key insight: Geineken has significantly higher EBITDA margin (21.4%) vs. Little Bud (5%). Reasons could be higher prices, lower costs, or both.

math.setup: Use Geineken revenue of $700M and apply cost percentages derived from the exhibit and brainstorming guidance. G&A = 10% of rev, Sales/Dist = 25% of rev, Marketing = 18.1% of rev.
steps: Geineken COGS: given as needed to reach Gross Profit. From Exhibit 3 context: COGS% ≈ 25.5%, so COGS = 700 × 25.5% = $178M
Little Bud EBITDA margin = 5/100 = 5%; Geineken EBITDA margin = 150/700 = 21.4%
math.answer: Geineken EBITDA = $150M (21.4% margin) vs. Little Bud $5M (5% margin). Geineken benefits from higher unit price ($110 vs. $100), lower COGS per unit ($28 vs. $30), and lower % costs in Sales/Distribution and Marketing due to scale economies.

questions.prompt: What are the sources of Geineken's cost advantages vs. Little Bud?
questions.guidance: Candidate should hypothesize before being told. Three key areas: (1) G&A — Little Bud has already exhausted G&A scale economies (same 10% ratio). (2) Sales & Distribution — due to market regulations on truck size, Geineken's larger market share means higher asset utilization. (3) Marketing — Geineken spends 5x more in absolute terms yet a lower % of revenue, gaining much greater reach and brand awareness per dollar of revenue.

questions.prompt: What strategic options does Little Bud have?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm and then evaluate each option critically: (1) Increase market share via product innovation — consumer taste is well-defined, no room for new products. (2) Price war — virtually impossible; Geineken can sustain losses that would bankrupt Little Bud. (3) Marketing competition — Geineken spends 5x more in absolute terms; not viable. (4) Further cost reduction — no additional opportunities. (5) Focus on niche/specialty beer — market is very small. (6) Move to related markets (soda, juices) — company has already analyzed and rejected this due to competition. Conclusion: selling the company to Geineken (or via open bid) is the strongest strategic option.

questions.prompt: How would you value Little Bud? What is Little Bud's standalone market value, and what is its value to Geineken?
questions.guidance: Candidate should propose at least DCF and EBITDA multiples. For a quick assessment with available EBITDA figures, use EV/EBITDA multiple. Interviewer provides: EV/EBITDA = 10x. Standalone value = 10 × $5M = $50M. Value to Geineken = apply Geineken's margin (21.4%) to Little Bud's revenues ($100M), giving EBITDA of ~$21.4M, then multiply by 10x = ~$214M. Actual synergy value may be higher because Geineken would become a monopoly and could raise prices and squeeze suppliers further.

math.setup: Standalone: EV = EBITDA multiple × Little Bud EBITDA. Value to Geineken: apply Geineken's cost structure to Little Bud's revenue base, then apply multiple.
steps: Geineken margin = 21.4%; apply to Little Bud revenue: $100M × 21.4% = $21.4M EBITDA
math.answer: Standalone value ≈ $50M; Value to Geineken ≈ $214M (potentially higher if Geineken gains monopoly pricing power).

questions.prompt: How could Little Bud maximize its sale price above $214M?
questions.guidance: Little Bud should run an open bid process to attract other potential buyers (e.g., large international beer companies). Geineken has a strong incentive to pay more than $214M to prevent a large international player from entering the market and disrupting its dominant position. Competition among bidders forces Geineken to bid above its minimum valuation.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks of selling Little Bud to Geineken?

categories.name: Regulatory / Legal
ideas: Antitrust agencies may block the transaction since it would create a monopoly
Regulatory approval process could be lengthy and uncertain

categories.name: Customer / Brand
ideas: Loyal Little Bud customers may react negatively to the acquisition
Brand identity and local heritage could be lost

categories.name: Employees / Culture
ideas: Jobs may be lost due to realized synergies, causing friction
Company cultures could clash and create integration problems

categories.name: Deal Execution
ideas: Geineken may be the only realistic bidder, limiting negotiating leverage
Valuation gap between standalone ($50M) and synergy value ($214M) must be bridged in negotiations

recommendation: Recommend that Little Bud's CEO sell the company

Little Bud has no sustainable competitive advantage — Geineken's scale economies in distribution and marketing, combined with higher unit prices and lower unit costs, mean Geineken could initiate a price war that would drive Little Bud to bankruptcy
By selling now, Little Bud shareholders can capture value far above standalone worth ($50M) by leveraging the strategic value to Geineken (~$214M or higher)
risks: Antitrust agencies may block the deal given the resulting monopoly
Geineken may be the only viable buyer, weakening Little Bud's negotiating position
Loyal customers and employees may react negatively
next_steps: Hire an investment bank to structure and run the sale process with an open bid
Evaluate antitrust risk and engage regulators early
Identify potential cost-saving opportunities as a contingency if Geineken responds by cutting prices before the deal closes
Identify and approach potential international acquirers to create competitive tension in the bid process
